title: Digestive enzymes table
subject: Science (GCSE Biology, Chemistry, Physics)
source: Seeded from gcse-science/y10 lesson 75 (Digestive enzymes table (portal worksheet))
intro: Lesson 75: Digestive enzymes and bile. To understand how digestive enzymes and bile break down food into molecules small enough to absorb

head: Neutralising acid
Emulsifying lipids
rows: Large droplets split into small ones
Raises pH from the stomach's acid
Enzymes in intestine work best at alkaline pH

questions.q: State where bile is made and stored. [2 marks]
questions.a: Made in the liver (1); stored in the gall bladder (1).
questions.model: Two places, two marks. Made: liver. Stored: gall bladder. Released into the small intestine (duodenum) after a meal.

questions.q: Name the products of protein digestion.
Name the enzyme that digests maltose.
Core: Complete the digestion table: enzyme, where made, substrate, products, for amylase, maltase, protease and lipase.
questions.a: Amylase (salivary glands, pancreas): starch to maltose; maltase (small intestine): maltose to glucose; protease (stomach, pancreas): protein to amino acids; lipase (pancreas): lipids to fatty acids and glycerol.
questions.model: Teacher fills amylase: made in salivary glands and pancreas; starch to maltose.

questions.q: Extend: Explain two ways bile helps digestion. [4 marks] Write in the portal response box.
questions.a: Bile is alkaline (1) so it neutralises stomach acid, giving a suitable pH for intestinal enzymes (1); it emulsifies lipids into small droplets (1), increasing surface area for lipase (1).

questions.q: Stretch: A person has their gall bladder removed. Suggest why they are advised to eat less fat.
questions.a: Bile cannot be stored and released in large amounts at mealtimes, so fat is emulsified less well.

questions.q: Big question: why does your body need both enzymes and bile for a fatty meal?
questions.a: Lipase digests lipids; bile emulsifies them and neutralises acid so lipase works faster.
